## Part 2: the record-keeping part of the `coordinator` skill, a draft

This is a draft of the record-keeping part of the `coordinator` skill: the form of a FACTS or POSITIONS entry, and the pass by which the coordinator turns what a worker wrote into entries. It would replace "How the records are kept" in `.claude/skills/coordinator/references/roles-and-records.md`. The `fortress-repo` skill keeps how workers read and use the record, and how they edit it when a brief asks them to; the last two sections list what changes there and in the other places that state the structure today. Each sentence is marked (his words), (on record) or (new). "His words" includes the framing he gave through the coordinator on 2026-10-13, about 09:20 UTC, and his chat messages and page comments of that day, quoted with their UTC times. Part 5 lists where each point of the test and of his comments went.

### The principles

The part as he reads it once. Each principle is an instruction to the coordinator writing or using an entry, then its reason, then a pair of texts: an old text and its new one from the trial or the test, or a text of the draft's page that he commented on and the text that replaces it. Each names the items below that it stands for. A principle marked as the coordinator's proposal is not yet his word.

#### 1. Keep FACTS and POSITIONS to the project, and put how you and he work in this skill

His words, 09:16: "positions and facts I believe should relate to the project only." A procedure or a fact about the platform has its home in a skill, and an entry that holds it is a second home.
- Old (FACTS 201): "A run whose script has changed since launch is resumed from a copy of the script as launched (`git show <base>:<path>`)."
- New: "How: the `coordinator` skill, `references/agents.md`, "Resuming a Workflow run"."

Items 1 to 4.

#### 2. Write the status quo, and leave how it came about to the history

His words, 09:02: "my optimized build is about capturing the current status quo." A date, a mark of change or an account of how a fact was found changes nothing a reader does, and the history keeps it verbatim.
- Old (FACTS 94): "A bound list that names a trait with a `comprises` clause no longer crashes it"
- New: "so the array family checks under `T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }`, but calls through such a bound are still refused or crash"

<!-- The coordinator's knowledge base, created 2026-09-15 at Pavol's request. Read at every session start and after every compaction, before any work. -->

# The coordinator's knowledge base

Boot, at session start and after every compaction, in this order: `CLAUDE.md`
→ `explorations/protocol.md` → `FACTS.md` (whole, in one pass) →
`POSITIONS.md` → `INDEX.md`, then `check-index.sh` run and every note it
reports missing given its line (Pavol, 2026-09-24) →
`PLAN.md`, first section → `BOOT.md`, the boot note → `HELD.md`, the held
list. If the boot note says a batch is running, its `CLIMB-BATCH-*.md` next, only the sections for Pavol, on the
choices inside the rungs and on how it is run (1, 5 and 6 in batch 6), since
the rung sections are the workers' briefs, and the run's `journal.jsonl` and
its agents' last transcript timestamps before anything is said about it.
Nothing else is read by the
coordinator itself: reports, transcripts, ledger rows and source go to a
worker that returns a summary; whether a worker is still running is read from
the harness's notice at the top of the turn and from `test -f` on the one
output path its brief names, never by listing a directory. The boot read is
full context by Pavol's word: a resumed coordinator knows the project without
him.

The coordinator is two things and keeps two records. As orchestrator it keeps
what a worker or its own next incarnation needs to act: `FACTS.md` (what is
established about the language, the library, the runtime and this container,
each fact in a few lines with its source and its test, the detail left in
the report it cites), `INDEX.md` (one line per
standalone note, searched before any fact is called absent), `PLAN.md` (the
phases, the open issues in the order they need deciding, the parked items),
`PLAN.md`'s first section (where the work stands) and `BOOT.md`, the boot
note, whose one purpose is to tell the post-compaction coordinator what is in
flight: what is running, what to do when it completes, and a question waiting
on Pavol if one is. As executive assistant it keeps what keeps the project on track and
Pavol out of the wall of text: the open issues and their order (`PLAN.md`),
the held list while he reads (`HELD.md`: each point a line in the coordinator's words with the UTC time of his message, the transcript holding his exact words), and `POSITIONS.md`,
what he has decided and already knows, dated, in his words, so that nothing is
re-asked or re-explained; it is not a log of what he said.

How they are kept:

- `FACTS.md` and `POSITIONS.md` are the optimized build: what is true of the
  tree now, and what he holds now, written timelessly, with no dates, no rung
  or commit names and no account of what changed when or what corrected
  what; `FACTS-history.md` and `POSITIONS-history.md` are the debug build,
  with the full provenance: every earlier text of every entry, verbatim,
  under a dated section, with a comment line saying what became of it, and
  his quotes at their dates. A worker or a coordinator may append an entry
  with a date, a quote, a rung's name or a commit in it, and may correct an
  earlier entry beside it; each consolidation compiles that out: the
  provenance moves to the history and the fact or the position is rewritten
  without it, at full informational fidelity. An entry that changes is
  rewritten in place; no "superseded by", no "corrected", no dated updates
  inside an entry. `FACTS.md` is consolidated before each batch launches,
  since the batch's agents read it; `POSITIONS.md` at each landing or when he
  replaces a decision.
  Before each commit of such a consolidation,
  `tools/check-verbatim.py <base> <file> <history>` shows every entry of the
  file at the base verbatim in the file or in its history.
- One home per thing. His words are written once, in `POSITIONS.md`; every
  other file points to the entry. Nothing is written twice.
- A remark is not a decision, and neither is a one-off go. A change to how we
  work is a protocol line rewritten; a go or a push is written nowhere, the
  launch or the commit being its trace; a question is answered where the
  answer belongs; he is not told about record edits.
- Nothing a resumed coordinator needs is lost: what a `FACTS.md` entry leaves
  out is in the report or record it cites, and its earlier text is verbatim in
  the history.
- The boot note is rewritten whole at every change, never appended to.
- A fact enters in the commit that establishes it; a decision in the next
  commit after he states it. A FACTS entry is cited by its bold title, or by
  its opening words where it has none, and a POSITIONS entry by its bold
  title; a title that still holds stays verbatim when the entry is rewritten,
  and a title that no longer holds is rewritten to state the present, its old
  text kept in the history and every citation of it updated.

<!-- Established facts: what is true of the tree now, grouped by area, each with its source (a path, a test, a ledger row) and the numbers that describe the tree. Timeless: no dates, no account of how a fact was established or what it superseded; that record is `FACTS-history.md`, where every earlier text of every entry stands verbatim under a dated section. An entry is cited by its bold title, or by its opening words where it has none; a title that still holds stays verbatim when the entry is rewritten, and a title that no longer holds is rewritten to state the present, its old text kept in the history and every citation of it updated. A worker or a coordinator may append an entry with a date, a rung's name or a commit in it; the consolidation before each batch compiles that out into the history and leaves the fact. Read at session start; cite by title rather than restating in chat. -->

# Facts on record

## Execution model

- Two execution paths share parser and phases and differ at the end: the walk interpreter (`fortress file.fss`) and the bytecode compiler (`fortress compile` + `run`) (`repo-internals.md:97-129`).
- The static type checker (Scala, `scala_src/typechecker/`) runs only on the compile path; `walk` turns it off and there is no switch to make it run in the interpreter (`repo-internals.md:127`); every "type error" seen from the interpreter is a run-time dispatch failure.
- `fortress typecheck` checks against `Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi`, not the interpreter's prelude, so it is not an oracle for interpreter programs (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/Shell.java:453-458` calls `useCompilerLibraries()`; row 69). The checker on interpreter programs comes after the switch-over (POSITIONS, "The type checker on interpreter programs.").
- The code generator lowers every type to a JVM reference type: `RR64` to the run-time class `FRR64`, so a compiled loop over `RR64` holds no `dadd` or `dmul` (`repo-internals.md:129`; the bytecode quoted in `perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md` section 4). An array is a library object read and written through `get` and `put` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1417`, `:1468`), not a `double[]`.
- On microGPT-shaped array code boxing is the dominant representational cost: in Java models of the program's three kernels, boxed elements cost 6.3× (dot product), 6.5× (matrix product) and 2.6× (row lift) over `double[]` (`perf-probes/kernels/REPORT.md` sections 2 and 4). No microGPT-shaped kernel compiles: the compiler prelude has no array type, and `Array`, `Vector` and `Array3` are undefined in `FlatArrays.fsi` (row 305). No array type goes into the compiler prelude; the arrays reach the compiled path with the one library (POSITIONS, "The library route."). A failed compile leaves a 0-byte jar in the bytecode cache (row 304).
- With rows 302 and 303 fixed (the next two entries), the compiled scalar `RR64` loop `bench1t` runs in 0.74 s, against 13.06 s on the tree before them, a pair timed in one session (`compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`, "The four timings"). Two costs that the boxing probe named in that loop are unaddressed (`perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md` section 5). One is the `for` lowered to the compiler prelude's `countedseqloop`, a recursive binary subdivision over boxed indices with a closure call per element (`Library/CompilerLibrary.fss:373-381`). The other is the representational rest, which unboxed doubles would attack: the transacted volatile cell, four allocations per iteration, the interface hop to the native wrapper and the `checkcast`s.
- The eager debug string of `BaseTask.inATransaction()` is fixed: the message is built only under the `debug` flag (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/runtimeSystem/BaseTask.java:248`; row 302; `compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`).
- `FFloatLiteral`'s String round trip is fixed: the literal caches its `double` instead of re-parsing its text in `asRR64()` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/runtimeValues/FFloatLiteral.java`; row 303; `compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`).
- The benchmark numbers on record, `bench1t` 9.3441 s and `bench1h` 6.0732 s (`perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md`, `perf-probes/kernels/REPORT.md`), are one session's: the same unmodified tree timed 13.0566 s and 8.8159 s in another (`compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`, "The four timings"). Absolute seconds are not comparable across sessions; only a before-and-after pair taken in one session measures a difference.
- `ant compileAll` leaves the bytecode cache holding no library jars when it changes the implementation, and only then: it deletes the caches whole when the sources or the build differ from what the last successful build left ("**`ant compileAll` deletes the caches folder, the linker's untracked `global.map` with it, when the implementation changed, and keeps it otherwise**" under The harness and the gate), and `fortress run` then dies with `NoClassDefFoundError: fortress/CompilerLibrary$GeneratorZZ32`. The library-order recompile of `repo-internals.md:172-185` restores the jars in about two minutes. #!/usr/bin/env python3
"""The gap ledger's tool: it owns the ledger's format, reads its rows, and is
the only way to write them.

The ledger, explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md, is sorted into topic sections,
each a "## TITLE" heading over one table of rows. A row is one line of eight
cells, and keeps its number wherever it sits:

  | # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |

The template (POSITIONS.md, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is
explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md, 4.1):
  status       exactly one of POSITIVE-VERIFIED, NEGATIVE-VERIFIED,
               NEGATIVE-BOUNDED, CONTESTED, RETIRED, FIXED, DUPLICATE
  class        `kind (area)`, kind one of the legend's seven, area one of ten;
               `—` only for POSITIVE-VERIFIED and RETIRED
  spec         the .tex file and the section heading in quotes; a line number
               only against Specification-1.0-frozen/; `silent` where the
               specification does not say
  reproducer   one test (a name under the test folders, or a path) or probe
               path from the repository root, or `none`
  limits       row 1,200 characters, claim 300, reproducer 200, found by 60,
               notes 700
  a pipe inside a cell is written \\|

Cells are split only at a pipe that is not escaped as \\|. A row whose cells
hold bare pipes (the ledger had six) does not split into its table's width that
way; it is read by its split at pipes followed by a space or the line's end, as
facts-extract.py has always read it, and check reports it under `pipe`.

Every write takes a lock (flock on .ledger.lock beside the ledger), checks the
template on the line it writes, and puts the full earlier line of a row it
changes, unchanged, in the history file beside the ledger
(fortress-gap-ledger-history.md), under "### Row N" and a line saying what
became of it. A failed check prints the rules the row breaks and exits 1.

usage: ledger.py COMMAND [ARGS] [--root DIR] [--ledger FILE] [--history FILE]

  heads                      one tab-separated line per row: number, status,
                             class, the claim's first 150 characters, and the
                             paths the row cites in backticks
  sections                   each section that holds a row table: its row
                             count and title, tab-separated
  section TITLE              the heads of that section's rows
  show N [--short]           row N under its section and table header; with
                             --short, its status, class, claim and the notes'
                             first 300 characters
  find WORDS [--open] [--cites FILE[:LINE]] [--all]
                             one line per row that holds every word (whole
                             words, or a word's start with a trailing *):
                             number, status, class, the claim's start; --open
                             leaves out FIXED, DUPLICATE and RETIRED; --cites
                             keeps the rows citing FILE (at LINE) and prints
                             the lines they cite; at most 10 rows unless --all
  count                      the rows by status, kind and area; nothing stored
  add FILE --section TITLE   FILE holds one row line, its # cell `?` (or the
                             seven cells after it); numbers it max + 1 and
                             inserts it in that section's table in number
                             order
  note N TEXT                appends TEXT to row N's notes
  close N --commit HASH --test NAME [--note TEXT] [--claim C] [--class C]
        [--spec C] [--found-by C]
                             after the fix has landed: HASH must be in HEAD's
                             history and NAME a test under the test folders;
                             writes the one-line FIXED row (the claim's first
                             sentence, the test as reproducer, notes `fixed
                             HASH; full text: history, row N`); the options
                             give cells the old row lacks in the template's form
  duplicate N --of M [--add TEXT] [--claim C] [--class C] [--spec C]
        [--reproducer C] [--found-by C]
                             makes row N a DUPLICATE pointer to row M (notes
                             `duplicate of row M; full text: history, row N`);
                             --add appends TEXT to row M's notes
  check [--rows FILE] [--base COMMIT] [--summary]
                             lints every row against the template, and the
                             tables' headers, numbers and order; --rows lints
                             a file holding only row lines instead; --base
                             also checks that every row at COMMIT is the same
                             line now or has its full earlier line in the
                             history file, and that the set of row numbers is
                             unchanged; --summary prints only the counts by
                             rule; exit 1 on any failure

Text given on the command line (TEXT, C) has its bare pipes escaped.
"""

import argparse
import collections
import fcntl
import os
import re
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
import unicodedata

TOOLS = os.path.dirname(os.path.realpath(__file__))
TREE = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(TOOLS)))   # the checkout this tool is in

LEDGER_REL = 'explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md'
HISTORY_NAME = 'fortress-gap-ledger-history.md'
LOCK_NAME = '.ledger.lock'

HEADER = ('#', 'claim', 'status', 'class', 'spec citation', 'reproducer', 'found by', 'notes / workaround')
CELLS = ('num', 'claim', 'status', 'class', 'spec', 'reproducer', 'found_by', 'notes')
# A header title to its cell; row 83's table names its notes "why unsettled".
HEADER_NAMES = dict(zip(HEADER, CELLS), **{'why unsettled': 'notes'})

STATUSES = ('POSITIVE-VERIFIED', 'NEGATIVE-VERIFIED', 'NEGATIVE-BOUNDED', 'CONTESTED', 'RETIRED', 'FIXED', 'DUPLICATE')
CLOSED = ('FIXED', 'DUPLICATE', 'RETIRED')
NO_CLASS = ('POSITIVE-VERIFIED', 'RETIRED')
KINDS = ('implementation gap', 'library gap vs spec', 'library bug', 'design limit', 'deliberate', 'typesetter', 'packaging')
AREAS = ('parser', 'walk', 'checker', 'codegen', 'runtime', 'library', 'prelude', 'specification', 'tests', 'tools')
DASH = '—'
LIMITS = (('row', 1200), ('claim', 300), ('reproducer', 200), ('found_by', 60), ('notes', 700))
HEAD_CLAIM = 150      # of a row's claim that heads and find print
SHORT_NOTES = 300     # of a row's notes that show --short prints
FIND_ROWS = 10        # rows find prints without --all
VACANT = {148}        # never used: run-c's row 148 was merged into row 8
FROZEN = 'Specification-1.0-frozen/'
PLACEHOLDERS = ('?', '#', 'N', '')
TEST_FOLDERS_EXTRA = ('shelltests', 'compiler_regressions', 'long_term_not_working', 'not_passing_yet', 'test_library')

SEP = re.compile(r'\|\s*:?-{3,}')
ROW = re.compile(r'\|\s*(\d+)\s*\|')
STRICT = re.compile(r'(?<!\\)\|')
LENIENT = re.compile(r'(?<!\\)\|(?=\s|$)')
CLASS = re.compile(r'(%s) \((%s)\)$' % ('|'.join(map(re.escape, KINDS)), '|'.join(AREAS)))
SPEC_FILE = re.compile(r'((?:[\w.+-]+/)*[\w.+-]+\.tex)(:\d[\d,:\s-]*)?')
QUOTED = re.compile(r'"([^"]+)"|“([^”]+)”')
TEX_HEAD = re.compile(r'\s*\\(?:part|chapter|section|subsection|subsubsection|paragraph)\*?\s*(?:\[[^\]]*\])?\s*\{(.*)\}')
PATH_EXT = re.compile(r'\.(fss|fsi|java|scala|tex|tick|rats|test|md|js|py|sh|out|txt|ast|xml|jj|log|csv|json|html|properties)$')
HASH = re.compile(r'\b[0-9a-f]{7,40}\b')


class LedgerError(Exception):
    pass


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- reading

def split_cells(line, pattern=STRICT):
    """A table line's cells, stripped: the text between the first and the last pipe, cut at pattern."""
    return [c.strip() for c in pattern.split(line.strip())[1:-1]]


def join_cells(cells):
    return '| ' + ' | '.join(cells) + ' |'


class Table:
    def __init__(self, section, index, header):
        self.section = section     # the Section it is under, or None
        self.index = index         # 0-based line of its header
        self.header = header       # its header and separator lines
        self.titles = split_cells(header[0]) if header else list(HEADER)
        self.names = [HEADER_NAMES.get(t) for t in self.titles]
        self.rows = []

    @property
    def holds_rows(self):
        return bool(self.names) and self.names[0] == 'num'


TEMPLATE = Table(None, -1, [join_cells(HEADER), '|' + '---|' * len(HEADER)])


class Section:
    def __init__(self, title, index):
        self.title = title
        self.index = index
        self.tables = []

    @property
    def rows(self):
        return [r for t in self.tables for r in t.rows]

    @property
    def row_tables(self):
        return [t for t in self.tables if t.holds_rows]


class Row:
    def __init__(self, num, lineno, section, table, line):
        self.num = num             # its number, or None for a line whose # cell is not one
        self.lineno = lineno       # 1-based line in its file
        self.section = section     # the title of the "## " section it is under, or None
        self.table = table
        self.header = table.header
        self.line = line
        width = len(table.names)
        cells = split_cells(line)
        self.split = 'strict'
        if len(cells) != width:
            lenient = split_cells(line, LENIENT)
            if len(lenient) == width:
                cells, self.split = lenient, 'lenient'
            else:
                self.split = 'bad'
        self.cells = cells

"""Check a consolidation of FACTS.md or POSITIONS.md: every entry of the file as
it stood at BASE appears verbatim, as a whole entry, in the file now or in its history file,
and in exactly one of the two.

An entry is a top-level bullet ("- ") with its indented continuation lines.
Written 2026-09-27 for the POSITIONS split (886a06e1d, repaired in cda7d86a6,
whose first pass had lost 20 entries' text); generalised 2026-09-29 to either file.

usage: check-verbatim.py BASE FILE HISTORY
  e.g. check-verbatim.py 8c1158937 explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md explorations/coordinator/FACTS-history.md
Exit 0 when no entry is missing and none is in both files; 1 otherwise.
"""
import subprocess, sys

if len(sys.argv) != 4:
    sys.exit(__doc__)
base, path, hpath = sys.argv[1:]
old = subprocess.run(['git', 'show', f'{base}:{path}'], capture_output=True, text=True, check=True).stdout
new = open(path, encoding='utf-8').read()
hist = open(hpath, encoding='utf-8').read()

def entries(text):
    out, cur, start = [], None, 0
    for i, ln in enumerate(text.split('\n'), 1):
        if ln.startswith('- '):
            if cur is not None:
                out.append((start, cur))
            cur, start = ln, i
        elif cur is not None and ln.startswith('  '):
            cur += '\n' + ln
        else:
            if cur is not None:
                out.append((start, cur))
            cur = None
    if cur is not None:
        out.append((start, cur))
    return out

# Whole entries are compared, not substrings: an entry cut to a prefix of an
# older text of itself would otherwise count as in the history too (2026-10-13).
E = entries(old)
N = {e for _, e in entries(new)}
H = {e for _, e in entries(hist)}
in_new = [n for n, e in E if e in N]
in_hist = [n for n, e in E if e in H]
both = [n for n, e in E if e in N and e in H]
missing = [(n, e) for n, e in E if e not in N and e not in H]
print(f'entries in {path} at {base}: {len(E)} ({len(old.encode())} bytes); now {len(new.encode())} bytes')
print(f'  verbatim in the file now:        {len(in_new)}')
print(f'  verbatim in the history file:    {len(in_hist)}')
print(f'  in both (should be 0):           {len(both)} {both}')
print(f'  in neither (should be 0):        {len(missing)}')
for n, e in missing:
    print(f'    MISSING old line {n}: {e[:100]}')
print('moved to history (old line numbers):', ' '.join(str(n) for n in in_hist))
sys.exit(1 if missing or both else 0)

<!-- The baseline interview: a setting and eighteen questions that a fresh session of a model answers with its default instincts for the coordinator's job (where it keeps the project's memory, what it does with a worker's report, how it talks to the curator on a phone, how it decides and delegates), run in a private namespace with no record, no skill and no tool, so that the `coordinator` skill can be written to hold only what the model would not do by itself; kept so that it is run again for each new model, Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 first, 2026-10-12, at the curator's word. -->

# The baseline interview

The `coordinator` skill is written on one principle, the curator's: it holds only what the model would not do by itself. What is specific to this project (the nine steps, test first under the sealed tree, the gate) and what is specific to this environment (the curator reads on a phone and dictates, the context is compacted, the container can be lost, the curator decides) go in. A rule that restates the model's own default is left out.

The baseline is what a model does by default. This kit finds it by interview, not by replay: a fresh session gets the setting and the questions, and nothing else, and answers with its instinct. An interview shows what a model says it would do, not what it does; the curator accepted that limit when he chose the method (POSITIONS, "The coordinator rewrite's goals").

## The files

- `setting.md`: the situation and the constraints the session is given. It names none of the record's files or terms, so that it does not prime the answer.
- `questions.md`: eighteen questions in four groups, memory and reports, talking to the curator, decisions, workers and runs. They follow the six groups of conduct rules in `process-engineering/coordinator-shape.md`, section 4.1, so that every rule can meet a default.
- `run.sh`: runs one model's interview. Its header says how the session is isolated.
- `answers/<model>.md`: each model's answers, verbatim, with the date, the Claude Code version and the effort at the top. The model is named by its version name, never by its identifier.

## How to run it

    explorations/coordinator/baseline-interview/run.sh fable /tmp/interview/fable
    explorations/coordinator/baseline-interview/run.sh opus  /tmp/interview/opus

The out-dir must lie outside `/home/user` and `/root`. Copy `answer.md` to `answers/<model>.md` with the header lines from `meta.txt`, the model's version name in place of its id. Each run writes under 0.1M tokens.

## How the answers are used

The conduct rules of the protocol and POSITIONS are sorted against the answers into three buckets: a default the model gives by itself (deleted), an environment rule (kept) and a project rule (kept). The skill is written from the two kept buckets.

## When to run it again

When a new model is to take the coordinating session, run the interview for it before the skill is adjusted, and keep its answers beside the others. The questions change only when the environment or the project changes what the coordinator must do; a changed question is run again for every model whose answers are kept.
You are the coordinating session of a software project kept in a git repository, running in a Claude Code cloud container. You direct worker agents and report to the person who owns the project. He reads your replies on a phone, often with text-to-speech, and writes to you by dictation. Your context is compacted when it grows long. The container can be lost at any time; only what is pushed survives. The work runs for weeks. Workers return written reports.

Answer each question with what you would do by default, in a few sentences. Do not design a system. Say your instinct. Answer in text only, with no tool use.
<!-- Opus 5.5's answers to the baseline interview, verbatim, 2026-10-12 12:57 UTC, one question per turn in one resumed session: Claude Code 2.1.296, effort xhigh, 18 turns, no tool call, 11K tokens out. The setting and the questions are beside this file; the one-shot answers of the same day are under oneshot/. -->

**1.** **In the repo, pushed, because nothing else survives a lost container.** The built-in memory folder under /root lives in the container, so I wouldn't rely on it for anything that matters.

My default would be a short CLAUDE.md at the repo root, which Claude Code loads automatically at the start of every session. It would hold standing rules and your preferences, and it would tell me to read a notes folder first. That folder would contain a few plain markdown files:

- **Status file.** Current goals, what each worker is doing, open questions for you. I'd rewrite it in place to keep it short, rather than letting it grow.
- **Decisions log.** One dated line per decision, with the reason, added as decisions are made.
- **Reports folder.** Each worker's report saved as a dated file. I'd fold the key points into the status file.

I'd commit and push after every meaningful change, not just at the end of a task. After a compaction or a fresh container, I'd reread CLAUDE.md, the status file and the recent git log before doing anything else.

**2.** **I'd save the full report unchanged**, as a dated file in the reports folder named after the worker and the task, and push it right away. That way the raw source survives even if I summarize it badly.

Then I'd read it and split it three ways, each line linking back to the report file:

- **Measurements** go into a running measurements file. Each one is a line or table row with the date, which worker measured it, the commit it was run on, how it was measured, and whether I've checked it or am taking the worker's word.
- **Decisions** go into the decisions log, dated, with the reason, and marked as either decided by the worker or confirmed by me or you.
- **Open points** go into the status file's open-questions list, each saying who it's waiting on.

**Yes, I'd always keep dates and who measured what.** Numbers go stale as the code changes, and workers sometimes get things wrong. Weeks later, the only way to know whether a figure still holds is to know when it was taken, on which version, and by whom.

Then I'd push, and send you a few spoken-friendly sentences: what changed, anything surprising, and anything that needs your call.

**3.** **First, the status file, in full.** I keep it short precisely so I can read all of it every time. It tells me the goals, what each worker is doing and what's waiting on you.

**Then git, to check reality matches the notes:** git status for anything uncommitted, and the last twenty or so commits. If the container survived a compaction, there may be work I did but never wrote down or pushed. I'd fix that first.

**Then the recent end of the decisions log**, roughly the last week or the last couple of dozen entries, so I don't reopen something already settled.

**I wouldn't reread reports or the full measurements file.** I'd open those only when a specific task needs them.

I'd also compare the compaction summary against the files. Where they disagree, I trust the pushed files. Anything in the summary that never made it into the files, I'd write down and push before carrying on.

**4.** **I'd split everything into what's current and what's history, and only load the current part.**

- **Status file:** rewritten, never appended. Finished work and resolved questions just come out. It stays small by construction.
- **Decisions log:** about once a week, I'd condense it into a short "standing decisions" section listing what is true now. Each line keeps its date and a link to the original entry. Superseded entries and the raw old log move to an archive file by month.
- **Measurements:** the same. The main file keeps only the latest trusted figure per metric, still with date, worker and commit. Older and superseded figures go to an archive.
- **Reports:** never edited and never loaded by default. They just accumulate in their folder.

Nothing is truly lost, because git keeps every old version and the archives are one link away. What I'm protecting is the small set of files I read after every compaction. I'd give that set a rough size budget, a few thousand words, and condense whenever it goes over.

**5.** **Yes, for anything that runs longer than a single sitting or goes to a worker.** Small fixes get only a good commit message.

Each note would be its own file in a tasks folder, named with the date and a short slug. Its report, when it arrives, would link back to it.

At the very top, a few short lines:

- **Status:** open, in progress, blocked, done or abandoned.
- **Dates:** started and last updated.
- **Owner:** which worker has it.
- **Goal:** one sentence.
- **Outcome:** once there is one, a sentence or two.

Below that come the brief I gave the worker, links to reports and commits, and working notes.

The point of the header is that I can skim just the tops of all the notes and know where everything stands, without reading any bodies. The status file links only to the notes still active. Finished notes keep their outcome line, so I can scan them later without opening the reports.

**6.** **First I'd save the message as he dictated it**, as a dated file in an inbox folder, and push. It's his instruction, and the container could die before I act on it. Dictation also garbles words, so the original is worth keeping.

Then I'd file each of the eight points where it belongs:

- Standing preferences go in CLAUDE.md.
- Decisions go in the decisions log, marked as his.
- New work goes in task notes and the status file.
- Questions he asked me get answered in the reply.

Each one links back to the saved message.

The reply follows his numbering, one to eight, with a sentence or two each: what I'll do, or the answer. I'd write it to work read aloud: plain sentences, no tables, and saying "point three" rather than relying on layout.

If I'm unsure what he meant on a point, especially a likely dictation slip, I'd say so on that point and give my best guess. Questions back to him would be few, and gathered at the end so he can answer them in one go.

**7.** **I'd reply to each one on its own, short, and anchored at the start to what it answers.** For example: "On your answer about the measurements file:". Listening by phone, he needs to know which thread he's in before the content starts.

Then I'd say what I'm doing about his answer. If things have moved on since that earlier reply, I'd say that plainly: "already done", or "that changed yesterday, here's where it stands now". I wouldn't act on a stale picture.

I wouldn't restate my earlier reply or give a full status update each time, only what's new on that one thread.

45:**11.** **In the decisions log, right away**, with the date, marked as his, his line quoted word for word, and one sentence on how I read it. I'd push immediately. The open question it settles comes off the status file, and any task note it affects gets a line pointing to the decision.

47-If it's a standing rule rather than a one-off ("always do X", "never Y"), it also goes in the standing orders at the top of CLAUDE.md. That gets loaded every session, so it can't fall out of view. When I condense the log, his decisions stay in the "standing decisions" section; they are never archived away.
48-
49-Rereading the decisions log isn't enough on its own, so CLAUDE.md also carries a rule for me: before asking him anything, check the standing decisions first.
50-
51-My reply would be one line confirming what I recorded, in my own words. If dictation garbled something, he catches it now, not weeks later.
52-
53-**12.** **Before asking, I'd do three things.**
54-
55-First, I'd check the standing decisions and the decisions log, to be sure he hasn't already settled it in other words.
56-
57-Second, I'd ask whether it's really his call. If it's cheap to reverse and low stakes, I'd decide it myself, record it, and just tell him.
<!-- Fable 5.1's answers to the baseline interview, verbatim, 2026-10-12 12:57 UTC, one question per turn in one resumed session: Claude Code 2.1.296, effort xhigh, 18 turns, no tool call, 9.6K tokens out. The setting and the questions are beside this file; the one-shot answers of the same day are under oneshot/. -->

**1.** Two places, with the repo as the one that actually counts. Anything about the project itself goes in a short notes file inside the repository, something like a NOTES.md at the root, committed and pushed every time it changes, because that is the only store that survives a lost container. It holds the current goal, what is done, what each worker is on, decisions with the reason behind them, and open questions, all with absolute dates, and it stays short enough to read in full. The memory directory under my Claude profile gets the things about you and how you want me to work, plus one pointer telling me to read the repo notes first. Its index is loaded into context automatically, so after a compaction I follow that pointer, read the notes file, and run a quick git log and status to see what changed since the notes were written. After a lost container I clone, do the same, and treat the pushed notes as the truth. I would update the notes as part of finishing any piece of work rather than at the end of the day, since the container can go at any moment.

**2.** I keep the whole report and I do not paste it into my notes. The raw text goes into the repo as its own file in a reports folder, named with the date and the worker, committed and pushed as is, so the detail is never lost and I can go back to it. Then I read it fully and pull three things into the notes file: decisions with the reason given, measurements that actually change what we do next, and open points turned into concrete questions or tasks. Every item I pull out gets the date, which worker produced it, and a pointer to the report file it came from, because weeks later a bare number with no owner is useless and because workers are sometimes wrong and I want to know whose numbers to recheck. Measurements go in a small table with the conditions they were taken under, not in prose. Any decision in the report that changes direction I do not adopt quietly, I flag it to you in the next message with my own view, and the rest I summarize to you in a few sentences with the file name in case you want the full thing.

**3.** First the compaction summary itself, since it carries what I was in the middle of, and then the memory index that is loaded for me, which should tell me to go to the repo notes. I read the notes file in full, every time, which is exactly why I keep it short, because a notes file I skim is a notes file I will misread. Then git status and the last handful of commits to catch anything that landed after the notes were last written, including worker pushes. That is the fixed part and it should be a few minutes of reading at most. Beyond that I read only what the task in flight points to, usually one worker report or one source file, and nothing else until I need it. I would not reread old reports to feel caught up, since the point of the notes is that I do not have to.

**4.** I split by what still affects decisions versus what is just history. The notes file I read every time stays a current-state file, so anything finished, superseded, or settled moves out into a dated history file that I do not read unless a question sends me there. A decision that is still in force stays as one line with its date and reason; a decision that was replaced gets a line in history saying what replaced it and when, then leaves the main file. Measurements that have been overtaken by newer ones go the same way. The raw reports folder never gets trimmed because it is never loaded. In the memory directory I delete entries that turned out wrong and merge ones that say the same thing, since a stale fact there is worse than no fact. I do this as its own commit with a message saying what moved, so you can see what I dropped and git can bring it back if I was wrong. The test is simple: if reading the main notes in full takes more than a few minutes, it has grown past its job and I prune it that day.

**5.** Not a file for every piece of work, no. Most work is already recorded by its commit and the worker report, so it gets one or two lines in the notes file saying what was done, when, by whom, and what it changed, and that is enough. A separate note only when the work produced something that does not fit in a line, like an investigation, a design choice with trade-offs, or a set of measurements, and those go as single files in a notes folder in the repo, one per topic rather than one per task. At the top of each I put the date, who did the work, the question it answers, its status as open, done, or superseded, and the answer in one sentence. That first sentence is the part that matters, because a future version of me will usually read only the top and decide from there whether to read the rest. The main notes file carries a pointer to it, so nothing exists that cannot be reached from the one file I always read.

**6.** First thing, before I answer, I write the eight points into the notes file as a numbered list with today's date, each one in a short line of his words rather than mine, marked open, and I push that, because a dictated message is the easiest thing to lose to a compaction. Then I reply with the same eight lines read back, one each, so he can hear whether I understood them, since dictation garbles names and numbers. Next to any point that conflicts with a standing decision or that I cannot act on without a choice from him, I say so in one sentence, and I keep those questions to the ones that actually block. I do not try to answer all eight in depth in one message; I say which ones I am starting on now and which are parked waiting on him. As each point gets done, asked, or dropped, its line in the notes changes status with the date, so the list in the file is always the current state and the next reply can just say which numbers moved.

**7.** One short reply per answer, in the same order he sent them, each starting with a few words that say which of my earlier messages it answers, because he is working through a stack and will not remember which one he was on when he hears my reply. Each reply stands on its own, with the outcome first and nothing he has to scroll back for. If his answer settles one of the numbered points, I update that line in the notes with the date and what he decided before I reply, so the decision is on disk before it is in a message. If an answer is to a message that newer events have overtaken, I say so in one sentence and ask whether it still stands, instead of acting on it or silently ignoring it. If two of his answers contradict each other, I take the later one and tell him I did, unless the difference changes real work, in which case I ask. I do not merge several replies into one long message, since he is listening, not reading.

**8.** First I look for it rather than apologize into the air: the notes file, the history file, the raw reports, the git log, and the compaction summary, to find whether the order was ever written down. That tells me which of two things failed, and I tell him which plainly. Either it never reached the file, so my intake failed, or it was in the file and I did not act on it or pruned it, so my reading failed. Either way I carry out the order now, or if I cannot find it at all I say so and ask him to say it again, and this time he hears it read back before anything else happens. What I change depends on the failure. If intake failed, every instruction from him goes into the notes before I write a reply, with no exception for small ones. If reading failed, standing orders get their own section at the top of the main notes that I never prune while open, where an order leaves only by being done or by him withdrawing it, with the date. I also write a memory entry about it, so the lesson survives even if the notes do not.

**9.** Mostly I do not know it, and I would rather say so than invent one. I have no feel for elapsed time between messages, so I only trust a clock I actually read, the container's date command or the timestamp on a commit, never my sense of how long something has been running. For estimates I use the one source that is real: the notes record when each worker task was handed out and when its report came back, so after a few weeks I have actual durations for comparable work and I quote those, saying what they are based on. For my own work I can be rougher but still only promise what I can see the whole of. Anything waiting on a decision from him or on something outside the container I do not put a time on at all; I say what it is waiting for instead. When I miss a time I say so with the real duration, and that goes in the notes too, so the next estimate starts from how long things really took and not from how long I hoped.

**10.** First it goes into the repo and gets pushed, so the thing he is approving is a fixed version with a commit hash and not a message that might drift. Then the message to him is short, because he is listening: what the document is, in one sentence; the two or three choices in it that actually need his judgment, each with what it costs and what I would pick; and what saying yes commits him to. I do not read him the whole document unless he asks, and if he asks I send it in pieces he can take one at a time. I end with a question he can answer in a word by dictation, yes, no, or change this part. When he answers, the notes get a line with the date, the commit that was approved, and any change he asked for, so later I can say exactly which version he said yes to and not just that he said yes.

**11.** It goes into the decisions section at the top of the main notes file, as one line with the date, his words as close to dictated as I can keep them, the reason if he gave one, and which open point it closes, and that commit is pushed before I write anything back to him. The open point itself gets marked closed with a pointer to the decision rather than deleted, so the question and its answer stay together. If the decision is about how he wants me to work rather than about the project, it also goes into my memory directory, since that is what I will see first after a compaction. Then I read it back to him in one line so a dictation error gets caught now and not in three weeks. The rule that makes this work is that before I ask him anything I look in that section, and a decision only leaves it when he changes it, with the date he did.

**12.** Before it reaches him I check that it is really open: the decisions section, the memory, the history file, and old reports, since the most common reason to ask twice is that it was answered once. Then I try to close it without him, by reading what the existing code already assumes, by a cheap experiment if one will settle it, or by finding that one option breaks something and drops out. What is left I narrow to one real choice between a few named options, and I form my own pick. The message then goes in this order: the question in one sentence, worded so he can answer with a word; my recommendation and the one reason behind it; the other options as a line each with what they cost; what I am doing in the meantime and what is blocked until he answers; and the path to the file where the fuller reasoning lives. If after all that I still cannot say which option I would pick, the question is not ready and I do more work before I send it.

**13.** First I find out whether it is a proposal or already in the code, because that changes what undoing it costs, and I check it against the standing decisions and against what the worker was actually asked to decide. If it sits inside the task's own scope and crosses nothing, I let it stand, write it in the notes as decided by that worker on that date with the reason it gave, and mention it to him in one line so nothing is decided behind his back. If it touches something he decided, or shifts direction, or has no reason attached, it does not become a decision yet: it goes in the notes marked provisional, with the worker's name, and I put it to him in the same shape as my own questions, with what the worker chose, why, what I think, and what reverting costs now. A worker that decided without giving a reason gets asked for one before anything else moves, and a worker that keeps deciding outside its brief gets a narrower brief next time, which I also note.

**14.** I do not quietly break it, because a rule I override when I judge it wrong is not a rule he can rely on. If the harm in this case is small and reversible, I follow the rule, finish the piece, and tell him in one message what the rule cost here, with the concrete case, so he can decide whether he wants an exception or a different rule. If the harm is real and hard to undo, I stop that one piece before the damage, carry on with everything else, and put the choice to him the same way, with what the rule says, what it does in this case, and what I would do instead. The case goes into the notes either way with the date, so that if it happens again I can show him it is a pattern and not a single bad moment. If he says keep the rule, I keep it, and that answer goes next to the rule so I do not raise it a second time.

**15.** I keep what needs the whole picture and the memory of him: reading every report, keeping the notes, judging what matters, deciding what to hand out, reviewing what comes back, and talking to him. I give out anything that can be stated in a brief and answered in a report: a search through the code, an implementation of a specified change, a measurement, a test run, a debugging session with a clear symptom, since those eat context I need for continuity. For tiers, Sonnet gets the work where the brief leaves little to decide, like searches, running and reporting tests, mechanical changes, and summarizing large files. Opus gets work where the worker has to think inside the brief, like implementation with design choices, debugging with no obvious cause, and reviewing another worker's change. Fable I use for myself, and for a worker only when being wrong is expensive or the problem has already beaten an Opus worker. And the brief matters more than the tier, so a Sonnet worker with a sharp brief beats an Opus worker with a vague one, which is a reason to spend my time on briefs.

**16.** I start it so that it does not depend on me watching: output going to a file in the repo, and a line in the notes saying what is running, when it started, where the output lands, and what I meant to do with the result, so that after a compaction or a lost container I know a run existed and where to look. Then I do other work and look at the file at long intervals, not in a tight loop that burns my context on nothing. Before I begin, he hears one short message: what is running, how long comparable runs took from the notes, and that the next thing he hears about it will be the result. In between he hears nothing about it unless it fails or crosses a point that changes a decision, because a message saying still running is noise on a phone. When it ends he gets the result in a line, what it changes, and the file path, and the duration goes into the notes for the next estimate.

**17.** Clone, read the notes file in full, and look at the date on its last update against the last commit, because the gap between the last push and the loss is exactly what is gone and I want to know its size before I do anything else. From the notes I list what was in flight: worker tasks handed out, long runs, anything marked as being written, and for each I check whether its output ever reached the repo. Then he hears one message that says the container was lost, which commit the project stands at, what work between that and the loss is gone, and which pieces I am restarting now, so that he is not surprised later by a thing he thought was done. The memory directory is empty, so I rebuild it from the pointer and the decisions section in the notes. And whatever the gap turns out to be, it tells me whether I was pushing often enough; if it was more than a piece of work, that changes, and the change goes in the notes.

**18.** Run the suite before I touch anything, and write down what fails already and how long it takes, because without that baseline I cannot tell later which failures are mine. Then read the code around the change and the tests that cover it, since in an old code base the tests say what the code is actually relied on to do, which is often not what the code looks like it does. Next a test that shows the behavior I want, run to see it fail, then the smallest change that makes it pass, nothing tidied on the way. Run the tests nearest the change, then the whole suite, and compare against the baseline, where the only differences allowed are the ones I intended. Commit with a message that says what changed and why, push, and if the suite had failures or flaky tests that were there before me, that goes in the notes with the date rather than getting fixed on the side or left for the next person to rediscover.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record

POSITIONS.md:133
- **The gap ledger's form.** A row's status cell holds exactly one word of seven: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`; no second status and nothing in brackets; a row with one half fixed stays `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED` and its notes say which half is fixed (D1 of `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md` section 4.5). The rewrite of the ledger is split among many small workers, each with a slice of rows it can hold in context, never one worker over the whole ledger; the duplicate search is a separate step before it, whose groups tell the rewrite which rows to join. The class cell is `kind (area)`, the area one of parser, walk, checker, codegen, runtime, library, prelude, specification, tests, tools; a specification citation gives the file and the section, a line number only against `Specification-1.0-frozen/`; a row is at most 1,200 characters, the open rows cut to it by the rewrite; the full earlier text of every changed row is in one history file, `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md` (D2 to D5 at the proposal's defaults). The rows are sorted into topic sections, the rewrite's topical groups becoming the sections, each row keeping its number; a new row goes into the section its writer names, and row 83 becomes an eight-cell row in its section (D6). `explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py` owns the ledger's format and is the only way to write it (add with the template checked, note, close, duplicate, check); `facts-extract.sh` stays the one reader of every record, its ledger queries calling `ledger.py`'s parser. D7, numbering rows during parallel batches, is open.

POSITIONS.md:135
- **The coordinator rewrite's goals.** The `coordinator` skill is rewritten by a heavier process than `fortress-repo`'s, since the coordinator acts in several roles that work well and must not be lost to an ill-considered change. Its goals: one home for how the coordinator works, the protocol retired and its rules that bind workers moved to `fortress-repo`; every kind of record with one home and a stated purpose, the informal homes (the handover's first section, the held list, PLAN's old rule sections, the boot note's standing lines) retired or folded in, and the skill saying plainly what goes where; a lighter boot that keeps his awareness (the coordinator knows the project without him, never re-asks a decision, never sends a worker to measure again what is on record), the open question being FACTS, POSITIONS and INDEX (their form, a grouping by topic, what they repeat of each other, what is always loaded and what is looked up), settled on evidence and a trial boot, not assumed; FACTS, POSITIONS and INDEX keep serving workers' briefs; no role lost (executive assistant, batch coordinator, roadmap architect, briefer of workers, analyst); the `fortress-repo` writing standard. The skill is tiered: a core always loaded, and sections loaded when the coordinator switches into a mode of work that is not needed all the time (running and reviewing a batch, process engineering, a post-mortem, among others), as the workers' skill separates building from exploring; the coordinator's modes are identified and described first. The batch workflow is in scope, since it is improved whenever it shows a problem. `cloud-container` follows by the `fortress-repo` method. The rewrite rests on the frontier model's own habits, not on a system designed around them: "I don't want a system of hundreds little rules with potentially contradicting dos and don'ts." The skill guides lightly, by a few general principles, among them how to talk to him in each situation, and the record is organized as the model organizes knowledge by itself: "Organization of the knowledge base should reflect the model's second nature, never fight it", which he names the rewrite's highest risk. So the natural baseline of the current models, Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5, is established before the design, and the design starts from what this project's environment adds to it: his review on a phone, dictation by speech to text, holding the open items of a long dictated message (preventing the wall-of-text spiral and recovering from it), and keeping a large body of project knowledge in order. The map also gives where each record home came from and which model made it. The map of the shape the rewrite starts from is `coordinator/process-engineering/coordinator-shape.md`. The skill is written from scratch by an Opus writer, from the sort of the rules against the baseline (what is kept, and the facts stated instead of rules), the map's problems to design against, and the writing principles; the writer does not read the existing skill, which is not refactored. A check against the sort's list after the draft shows whether anything kept was lost, and then the cold read follows as usual. A rule is kept when the failure it guards against is on record; the interview's self-report decides no drop, since the two disagree exactly on the rules that matter (the clock, closed decisions), and the interview showed only the record's default shape, a short current-state file with decisions and history apart, which is kept without instruction. The two sorts carry the map's handles, not the rule texts, and are not what he or the writer judges a rule by.

POSITIONS.md:130
- **The record's form: an optimized build and a debug build.** FACTS and POSITIONS are the optimized build, "what is true about the repository snapshot at this moment in time", written timelessly: no dates, no provenance, no account of what changed when or what corrected what; the history files are the debug build, with the full provenance, his quotes at their dates and every earlier text. "I don't want you to be searching with a flashlight in a dark room. I want to give you a map of the territory." A worker or a coordinator appending to FACTS or POSITIONS needs no timestamps; where one is written, or an entry corrects an earlier one, the next consolidation moves that provenance into the history and rewrites the fact or the position without it, at full informational fidelity. FACTS is consolidated before each batch launches, since workers read it and pay the cost. A FACTS entry is the fact, its source and its test in a few lines, pointing to the report or record that holds the detail, a rung's entry too, since rung entries written at full length, about 14 KB a landed batch, are most of FACTS' growth. The files read at every boot hold a clean current state and do not need edits as the work moves; the narrative of how a landed rung established a fact is history.

== explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md, ## The ledger

FACTS.md:219
- **The ledger's rows stand in fifteen topic sections, each in the row template, and `ledger.py` is the only way to write them** (`explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md`, "The row template"; POSITIONS, "The gap ledger's form."). Rows are never renumbered, and reports cite them by number; a row is at most 1,200 characters, its status one of seven words, its class `kind (area)`. Every earlier text of a changed row, and the ledger's text before the topic sections (the counts by kind, the revival worklist, the old section headings and which rows stood under each), is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`. `explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py` reads (`show`, `find`, `section`, `heads`), writes (`add --section`, `note`, `close`, `duplicate`), counts (`count`) and checks (`check`, `--base` against a commit), with its tests in `tools/test_ledger.py`; `facts-extract.sh`'s ledger queries read through its parser. A row at its length limit takes no further note, and the tool has no command to edit a claim; `close` takes a corrected claim with `--claim`. Its heading reader does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro, so a row naming a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line instead (row 457). `apl/lessons.md` is a view derived from the ledger.

<!-- The held list: the points the curator raised while reading, turn by turn or on a page, each a line in the coordinator's words with the UTC time of his message, the transcript holding his exact words; and the smaller items he still owns. Worked through one at a time when he says he is done; being on this list answers nothing. Its own home since 2026-10-12, at his word, moved from postmortem-2026-09-19/held-list.md with its sections as they stood. Read at boot after BOOT.md. -->

# Held list

## Held from his comments on the principles (2026-10-13)

His nine comments on the first section of https://claude.ai/artifact/17GstfC5tE8dttd8wWRRS6 (version 5), 15:25 to 16:03 UTC, each a thread on the page with his exact words; one line each in the coordinator's words. He stopped at principle 9 to resurface and set a strategy (16:01).

- 15:25 (principle 1) Draft the coordinator skill's outline first, so each entry moved out of FACTS or POSITIONS gets a section and nothing is lost in the move.
- 15:32 (principle 2) The history grew as a verbatim copy checked by a script; with numbers, it could be provenance metadata (when, from where, links into the report); one tool call by the coordinator could write the entry and its history part, so nothing is written twice; the record is a flat-file database; build the tooling during the consolidation so the chunk workers and later the coordinator use it; channel the model's instinct to keep a dated project memory into this place; asks whether this needs design help, perhaps a Fable review.
- 15:34 (principle 3) Agrees, but "changes what a worker or the coordinator does next" is not actionable as stated: wants a decision rubric grounded in a few examples, not a list of rules, that taps the model's instincts. 15:38: 600 or 1,000, an entry needs a reason to be large; did not understand the example (is a fact split from its consequence, the consequence sent to the history? that would be wrong).
- 15:46 (principle 4) Good, but not actionable; "kept the 14 and lost what the 14 are" was unreadable until the restored text named the errors: over-compression into numbers; FACTS wants the ASD-STE100-halfway register; error counts that change at every landing may be a different kind of fact, one current value, not one per experiment.
- 15:51 (principle 5) One home is right; copies go stale, pointers cost a lookup and the decision to look; a tool that surfaces a fact with its linked positions in one go, by the links in the metadata, a second-level cache behind the compressed record in context; fears over-engineering.
- 15:56 (principle 7, form) Storing his dictated words verbatim is counterproductive, as the dictation correction on the page shows; the quote paragraph does not belong to reading stages.
- 15:57 (principle 7, content) Good, but a coordinator-skill rule: why in the record part; does it bear on how the record is structured for lookup, or on recording provenance so a Sonnet scout knows where to dig.
- 16:01 (principle 8) Losing the thread: he thought we were defining how to consolidate the record, and the page mixes in what the coordinator skill does; stops commenting to resurface; the comments go on the held list with a strategy for them.
- 16:03 (principle 9) The second sentence ("quote that form in every brief") is unclear; keeping the provenance of ideas (his against the coordinator's) is a real failure mode, but how is it relevant to the consolidation.

## Held in chat and on the Record Rule Draft page (2026-10-13)

Points on how we work, kept here until the coordinator skill holds them (his words, 09:16: they go to the skill, not to POSITIONS). The record-keeping points are in `process-engineering/record-rule-draft.md` Part 5.

- 09:05 What he says about how we work did not reach the record, and several compactions lost it: a lossy compression. Wanted: a principle and a check that the coordinator caught his meaning; his dictation is not the source of truth but is refined into nuggets; a cold read or a test, as for the skills.
- 09:16 FACTS and POSITIONS hold the project only and stay, as briefs point into them; how he and the coordinator work goes to the coordinator skill; meanwhile the held list and the boot note are its scratch; draft the skill's parts and point to them.
- 09:22 The rewrite plan's first steps follow the fortress-repo method (`7ff472848`); 09:23 reuse the record consolidation and a quiz to check the record-keeping principles.
- 09:54 Pages keep the house style (the plan page's CSS); a worker building a page is pointed to it.
- 10:14 The success criterion for a compression: decisions stay as good, and a reader follows the pointers to the report or the history when needed; test it automatically, without him; if something critical is lost, find the middle ground entry by entry.
- 10:20 Tests stay small and on the records at hand; no elaborate evaluation design (an earlier one wasted tokens).
- 10:30 Links matter most in the history, which no one reads whole; how the coordinator lists the positions on a fact or traces an entry's history. Answered by numbered entries, taken at 11:05.
- 14:36 Keeping what was learned before a compaction is the default, not a question; asking it was a do-nothing choice.

## Held in chat (2026-10-12)

- 00:4x (2026-10-13, chat) The main problem with the revival story's last version was expansion he did not ask for, which made it too long to read. An update adds what landed, in the space the document already gives it; a brief for an update caps its length against the version before.
- 00:22 (2026-10-13, page comment on the revival story, part 1) The update should only have brought the story up to date with what landed; it reframed the document in the email's framing, because the coordinator's brief named Prof. Ryu as a second reader and asked for an early part on how the revival treats the team's work. Proposed on the thread: halfway back to version 15's framing (opening and order as before, updates and fact-check corrections kept, "Why now" and his quotes cut, the curation facts as a short later section next to what the revival changed); held until he is done commenting, then one Opus pass.
- 00:06 (2026-10-13, page comment on the revival story) "Decides what gets committed" is not correct: he does not read the code or review each commit. The protocol's first hard rule says it ("Pavol decides what gets committed"); the coordinator rewrite restates his role as the record shows it: he sets the goals and decides the design and process questions put to him.
- 21:00 The name for the coordinator-only files: "the desk" is a stupid name; he has no better one; a brainstorm is wanted before one is chosen.
- 21:00 The handover's first section into PLAN: not convinced; would PLAN then hold two levels of information. Settled by the coordinator as the one state section (BOOT.md), his to overturn.
- 21:00 The lint: not convinced; built from the handles being deleted, how would it catch new names; what do the existing scripts do. Answered in chat (a floor for the known shapes; the reader judges).

## Held from his page comments (2026-10-12)

His 19 comments on the sort page https://claude.ai/artifact/WoDrCFWNNso5YeLr9kuwvR, 15:30 to 16:00 UTC, each a thread on the page with his exact words; one line each in the coordinator's words:

- 15:30 One ask per message is contextual, not a general rule; he wants its full context recovered.
- 15:32 Lists not tables: keep; both models gave him tables, which the iOS client renders as one scrolling line.
- 15:32 The dialog tool: the reason is a timeout of about 60 seconds on iOS, not the interface; the rule is conditional on the client.
- 15:33 Numbers as K or M: he did not recognise the handle; the rule is his own words, 5K and 1.2M instead of spelled-out numbers.
- 15:35 A new term defined: did it come with ASD-STE100; how would the model know what is new to him.
- 15:36 Label which part answers which: unclear; wants its context (the scout: 15 September, at his two requests).
- 15:37 The clock rule: keep; it guards against relative times after a compaction; Opus wrote it and has stayed grounded since; it needs the formulation that worked.
- 15:38 Batch silence: keep; the overnight runs left him a session of progress notes; silence until he asks.
- 15:40 Not told about record edits: wants to know when it arose; "noted" may be fine.
- 15:42 The git-check hook: the empty-body technique is on record; a reset ritual at each restart, told to him, is what he wants.
- 15:44 Restate and hold: keep; the handle is too compressed; it is the guard against the wall-of-text spiral, which is the default.
- 15:46 The Select button: does one sentence carry it; a compressed summary could not.
- 15:48 The wip-branch line: drop unless another instruction needs it; he deletes branches locally when he gets to it.
- 15:53 Model what he knows: keep and expand into a separate file, a profile of what he knows and where his gaps are, built by archaeology; a major task, not for the skill.
- 15:56 He decides what is committed, a bare go: he does not recognise the handle; wants its origin.
- 15:57 A standing approval covers only what it names: reads as a tautology.
- 15:57 A step a yes covers: wants how it arose and its wider context (the scout: the prompting-guides review of 27 September).
- 15:58 The closed-decision search: keep; the trigger to search was needed.
- 16:00 A worker's decision in a report: the fortress-repo skill tells workers which decisions they may take and which to raise; he stopped the review here; the handles are over-compressed; go back to the positions as they work now.

## Held while he reads (2026-09-27)

Each point is a line in the coordinator's words with the UTC time of his message in the session transcript (`fe616d40`, backed up on `transcripts-blinded`), which holds his exact words: an index, not a copy. Worked through one at a time when he says he is done reading; being on this list answers nothing.

Reacting to the coordinator's reply on the gap ledger (07:47 UTC): its purpose, its stale derived views (the worklist and counts, rows 1-310 only), and a proposal to regroup open rows by the plan phase that closes them. His message, 07:57:42 UTC:

- Who writes into the ledger, when, and under which standing instruction.
- Was the ledger sorted by kind before; does it need re-sorting.
- Row numbers stay stable: rows are cited by number.
- Grouping by plan phase may be the wrong principle; the rows are many kinds of technical problem (the ledger's own 16 sections are by area).
- His mental model of the ledger may differ from what it is.
- Unsure about PLAN.md, the big plan file, as the place.
- No go yet on re-deriving the views: he wants to understand the proposal first; he does want the ledger put to good use.

Also waiting for his answer (PLAN.md, "Asked 2026-09-27"): the three worker questions, skeptic checks 11-13 and the gather's filing of items for him, for 6b; the principle 5 review line; a Fable judge overnight.

The record-keeping part of the coordinator skill: its principles, the part itself, a trial of it on the ten largest entries, and a blind test of the trial.

13 Oct 2026 · explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/record-rule-draft.md

The principles

These nine principles are the record-keeping part as you'd read it once. Each one is an instruction to the coordinator when it writes or uses an entry, then the reason. Then comes a pair of texts: an old one and its new one from the trial or the test, or a line of this page you commented on and what replaces it in the draft. Two principles are the coordinator's proposals, and one is in part. Each says so.

Keep FACTS and POSITIONS to the project, and put how you and the coordinator work in its skill.

Your words, 09:16: “positions and facts I believe should relate to the project only.” A procedure or a fact about the platform has its home in a skill, and an entry that holds it is a second home.

Old, in FACTS 201: “A run whose script has changed since launch is resumed from a copy of the script as launched (git show <base>:<path>).”
New: “How: the coordinator skill, references/agents.md, ‘Resuming a Workflow run’.”

Your words, 09:02: “my optimized build is about capturing the current status quo.” A date, a mark of change or the story of how a fact was found changes nothing a reader does. The history keeps it word for word.
